sections.h2: Who bills and who values property in Warren County, Georgia?
sections.html:
Two offices in Warrenton split the work. The Warren County Tax Commissioner bills and collects the tax, and the Warren County Board of Tax Assessors sets the value that bill is built on. Both list 521 Main Street, Warrenton, GA 30828.

The commissioner's page describes an elected constitutional office that takes homestead applications, prepares the digest, mails bills, keeps the accounts and sends the money to the school system and local governments. It also collects on real estate, public utilities, motor vehicles, mobile homes and timber, and it will take a card payment over the phone. The assessors set values only, so a question about the amount owed goes to the commissioner and a question about the value goes to the assessors.

The assessors' page also warns owners that appraisal staff may walk onto a property to update records under O.C.G.A. 48-5-264.1. They arrive in a county vehicle and leave a business card if nobody is home.

sections.h2: What does Warren County look like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Warren County is a small rural county with fewer residents than it had in 2010, and the Census Bureau's housing figures describe a low-priced market. The Census Bureau counts a July 2025 estimate of 5,269 residents, down from 5,834 at the 2010 census and close to the 5,215 counted in 2020. Warrenton, Camak and Norwood are the places the county chamber names as home to local business.

  • Land area: 284.36 square miles, about 18.3 people per square mile in 2020.
  • Housing units: 2,687, with 72.2% owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $67,100 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median gross rent: $690, and the Census lists no building permits for 2025.

With values at that level, a tax balance carried over from earlier years can take a visible share of the sale price. Sorting out every open year before you list keeps a surprise from showing up at the closing table. The county site calls itself the gateway to rural Georgia, and its pages stress farming, nature and history over new development.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 add a few more details buyers will ask about: 2,097 households, an average of 2.43 people per household, and 93.8% of residents living in the same house a year earlier. Households with a broadband subscription came to 63.2%, which matters when a buyer plans to work from the property. Median household income was $44,289.

sections.h2: When is Warren County property tax due, and what if it is late?
sections.html:
Georgia's Department of Revenue says the official due date is December 20, and a county may move it to December 1 or November 15 or split it into installments. Ask the tax commissioner which date is printed on your bill, because the state default and a county resolution can differ. Each taxpayer gets 60 days from the postmark of the bill before interest starts, and penalties can follow on unpaid balances.

The Warren County economic page says taxes are levied as of January 1 by the City of Warrenton, Warren County, the Warren County School District and the State, with every property assessed at 40% of fair market value. That page prints a rate of 30.358 mills for 2017 and an effective rate of 1.21%, so treat it as history. Ask the tax commissioner for the current millage on your parcel, or read the county's five-year levy history, which the finance page says is posted under O.C.G.A. 48-5-32.

  • Real estate returns are filed January 1 to April 1, and skipping a return carries last year's value forward.
  • A mobile home needs a location permit within 30 days of placement and a yearly renewal between January 1 and April 1.
  • A refund claim for tax paid in error must start within three years of payment.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Warren County assessment?
sections.html:
File a written appeal with the Warren County Board of Tax Assessors, postmarked no later than 45 days after the mailing date of your assessment notice. The Department of Revenue says an appeal can rest on taxability, value, uniformity or denial of an exemption. Do not send the form to the state, since only the county board can receive it.

State form PT-311A makes you pick a route when you file. A Board of Equalization hearing is the usual path, and a hearing officer is limited to non-homestead real property valued above $500,000. Arbitration is the third option, and it requires a certified appraisal from you within 45 days of the board's acknowledgment.

A losing taxpayer has 30 days after the decision to give written notice of appeal to superior court. Before the court hears it, taxes must be paid at the amount of the last year in which they were determined to be due (O.C.G.A. 48-5-29). If the final value comes in at 85% or less of the earlier figure, the owner recovers litigation costs and attorney's fees under O.C.G.A. 48-5-311.

sections.h2: Is there a homestead exemption in Warren County?
sections.html:
Yes, the statewide homestead exemptions apply, and the Department of Revenue lists no local homestead exemption in this county. You may apply any time after the property becomes your primary residence, but the application must be in by April 1 of the first year you want the exemption. Missing that date counts as a waiver for the year.

The Warren County Tax Commissioner's page says the office handles homestead applications, so start there. Bring proof the home is your residence and ask what the office requires for age or disability exemptions. A buyer who plans to live in the house has to file a new application of their own, so remind them of the April 1 cutoff when the closing falls late in the year.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax when I sell a Warren County house?
sections.html:
The bill for the year follows the January 1 owner, so the seller and buyer divide it in the closing statement. Ask the Warren County Tax Commissioner for a written balance covering every tax year before the closing date, and give it to the closing attorney. If the home sits inside Warrenton, Camak or Norwood, confirm whether a city bill exists alongside the county bill.

  • Request balances for the county, school district and any city levy.
  • Ask whether any mobile home or timber account is tied to the same owner.
  • Keep proof of payment for three years in case a refund claim is needed.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Warren County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Warren County Tax Commissioner at 706-465-2231. The office is at 521 Main Street in Warrenton, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 189, Warrenton, GA 30828. Value questions go to the assessors at 706-465-3321.

faqs.q: How many days do I have to appeal my Warren County value?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the mailing date of the assessment notice, and the appeal must be postmarked by then. File it in writing with the Board of Tax Assessors. The state does not accept appeals.

faqs.q: Does Warren County have its own homestead exemption?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Revenue lists no local homestead exemption for the county, so owners use the statewide exemptions. Apply by April 1 of the first year you want the benefit.

faqs.q: What share of market value is taxed in Warren County?
faqs.a: Property is assessed at 40% of fair market value, according to the county's economic development page. Exemptions come off that assessed figure before the millage rate is applied.

faqs.q: Can I pay a Warren County bill by phone?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax commissioner's page says staff will take a card payment over the phone, and it also links an online payment option. Call 706-465-2231 to confirm what fees apply.
